title: Wire MikroORM into a NestJS app and prove fork-per-request
description: In your archive-api project, add app.module.ts with MikroOrmModule.forRoot(config) and a BookModule that uses MikroOrmModule.forFeature([Book]). Build BookController with GET /books and POST /books endpoints. Build BookService with an injected EntityManager. In the POST handler, log (em as any)['id'] to the console before persisting. Start the server and send two consecutive POST /books requests using curl or HTTPie. Submit a screenshot of your server logs showing two different EntityManager IDs printed for the two requests — proving that each request got a fresh fork of the EM.
modelAnswer:
The screenshot must show two distinct numeric IDs logged for the two POST requests — e.g., 'EM id: 2' and 'EM id: 3'. The IDs must differ, proving MikroORM's middleware forked a new EM for each HTTP request.
If both requests show the same ID: the RequestContext middleware is not wired up. Check that MikroOrmModule.forRoot includes autoLoadEntities: true and that the app uses MikroOrmModule's built-in middleware (NestJS integration registers RequestContext automatically — if you see one ID, you may have used orm.em directly instead of injecting EntityManager via the module).

title: @Transactional on controller vs service + L7/L8 callback
description:
This task combines NestJS transaction scope (L9) with migrations and embeddables from L7–L8.

Part A (L9): In 4–6 sentences explain why @Transactional() on a controller method is an anti-pattern, while on a service method it is idiomatic. Reference separation of concerns: what controllers should and should not own, and what belongs in a service.

Part B (L7–L8 callback): Your BookService.createWithLog() is decorated with @Transactional(). It creates a Book (with an Address embeddable on Author) and an AuditLog in one atomic operation. A migration later adds a NOT NULL column to AuditLog without a default. Describe step by step what happens to in-flight createWithLog transactions that were mid-flight when the migration ran. What does this tell you about the order of migration deployment vs service deployment in production?

Submit both parts as text.
modelAnswer:
Part A: Controllers are HTTP adapters — they translate HTTP requests into service calls and HTTP responses out of service results. They should not own any business logic or transactional state. Placing @Transactional() on a controller tightly couples the HTTP layer to the database transaction boundary, making it impossible to call the same logic from a queue handler or a cron job without going through HTTP. A service method decorated with @Transactional() is called by any client (HTTP, queue, cron) uniformly — the transaction boundary lives where the business operation begins.

Part B: If the migration adds a NOT NULL column to AuditLog without a default, any INSERT to AuditLog that does not explicitly supply that column will fail with a NOT NULL constraint violation. In-flight transactions started before the migration will continue against the old schema if they hold an open transaction (Postgres DDL acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — so typically the migration blocks until all active transactions on that table finish). After the migration commits, any new createWithLog call will fail until the service code is also deployed with the new column populated. Lesson: always deploy migrations that add NOT NULL columns in two steps — first with a DEFAULT, then (after service is deployed) remove the default.

title: Transactional Outbox — design, implement, stress-test (AI-resilient)
description:
Design and implement a minimal Transactional Outbox for the archive-api NestJS app. When a Book is created, an OutboxEvent entity (eventType, payload JSON, processedAt nullable) must be inserted in the same transaction as the Book INSERT. A background processor (a NestJS @Cron job decorated with @CreateRequestContext()) must poll for unprocessed events, process them (for this task: console.log the payload), and mark them processedAt.

Three-stage task:
1. Design: draw the entity relationship in pseudocode or a text table. What is the invariant this pattern guarantees? What problem does it solve that 'publish event after flush' does not?
2. Implement: wire it. Run two book creations and verify in the DB (via psql or a raw query) that two OutboxEvent rows exist with processedAt filled.
3. Stress test (text only, no code): describe what happens if the @Cron job crashes between reading and marking processedAt. Is the event processed twice or dropped? How would you make processing idempotent?

Metacognitive memo: What does the outbox pattern reveal about the boundary between ORM operations and message broker operations that a typical MikroORM tutorial misses?

title: Why does @CreateRequestContext() exist separately from the NestJS middleware?
description: The RequestContext middleware automatically forks an EntityManager for every HTTP request. @CreateRequestContext() does the same for non-HTTP execution contexts. Why can't queue handlers and cron jobs simply reuse the EM that the HTTP middleware creates? What is the entity lifecycle state of a 'stale' managed entity sitting in a long-lived EM that has not been forked for the current job run? Answer in 4–6 sentences.
